text: A leaked AWS access key or Azure service principal secret rarely leads straight to disaster. It leads to a surprisingly predictable sequence, and if you know that sequence cold, you can catch it long before it becomes a cost spike or a breach notice. This lesson walks through exactly how a leaked credential actually gets abused, grounded in patterns security teams see over and over in real incidents.

The leak itself is usually mundane. A developer commits an access key into a public GitHub repo, and automated secret-scanning tools can pick it up within minutes. Before IMDSv2 made a session token mandatory, a server-side request forgery flaw could reach an EC2 instance's metadata endpoint and pull its temporary role credentials directly. Plain phishing and malware still work too — harvest a session, or read the credentials file off a compromised laptop.

Once an attacker has a working credential, the first calls are quiet and read-only. get-caller-identity confirms who they are; list-attached-user-policies, list-buckets, and describe-instances map out what that identity can touch. In Azure, az account show and a few Microsoft Graph calls do the same job. None of this looks like an attack — it looks like automation, which is exactly why it's easy to miss.

From there, the sequence is enumerate, escalate, persist, act. If the leaked identity isn't already privileged, the attacker hunts for a path upward — next lesson's topic. Before touching anything destructive, they lock in persistence: a second access key or a new app registration secret, so rotating the original leaked credential doesn't end their access. Only then do they act — and one of the single most common documented outcomes is cryptomining on someone else's bill.

This sequence maps directly onto MITRE ATT&CK's Cloud matrix, the public catalog of real-world cloud attack techniques. Enumeration lines up with account and permission discovery. The leaked credential itself is a valid cloud accounts technique. Creating a second credential or a new account are both documented persistence techniques. Learning these technique IDs now means you can write an incident report another analyst immediately trusts.

The takeaway: every stage before the final payoff is detectable, and on its own, nearly invisible in terms of damage. A team that only watches for the cost spike is catching this after persistence is already locked in, which means rotating the original key alone accomplishes nothing. Next, we go deep on the escalation step — the specific, documented ways attackers climb from a low-privilege leaked credential to something far more dangerous.
